en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek has no verb in this clause.

01.r: The readers are told to look closely at Melchizedek's greatness.
01.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to look at, gaze, behold'. The same form could also be read as a statement, 'you see', but every translation here takes it as a command.

02.r: Moves the argument to its next point.

03.r: Calls attention to the size of Melchizedek's standing.
03.n: Abbott-Smith explains that the word properly asks about size, and files this verse under 'of personal greatness'; this is one of its two uses in the New Testament.

04.r: Melchizedek, the subject of the whole passage.
04.n: The BSB writes his name; the Greek says only 'this one'.

05.r: Melchizedek again, now as the one who received the tenth.

06.r: Stresses that Abraham, of all people, gave to him.
06.n: The KJV, Geneva and BSB read 'even', which brings out the force of the argument: even the patriarch gave. 'Also' is the plainer rendering, and the same word in Hebrews 7:2 is rendered 'also'.

07.r: The tenth part that Abraham gave Melchizedek.
07.n: The feminine of the adjective 'tenth', standing alone as a noun. This study renders it 'tenth' throughout Hebrews 7.

09.r: Abraham gave the tenth to Melchizedek.

10.r: Marks the spoils as the store from which the tenth was taken.

11.r: The particular spoils of the battle in the story.

12.r: The best part of what was taken in war.
12.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from 'top' and 'heap': properly the top of the heap, and so, in the plural, first-fruits, or in war the choicest spoils, the sense he gives for this verse. This is its only occurrence in the New Testament. The KJV and BSB say only 'spoils' and 'plunder'.

13.r: Marks the title that follows as Abraham's own.

14.r: Abraham as the founding father of the people.
14.n: The Greek holds this title to the very end of the sentence, which gives it weight: it was the patriarch himself who gave. Abbott-Smith gives its parts as πατριά and ἄρχω; in plain terms, the head of a family line.
